clue.text: Compete, but not have one sniff of blue cheese?

indicators.note: the clue says compete but without one, so a numeral one is struck from the verb

parts.note: to compete is to vie
one is the Roman numeral I
to sniff is to nose, as in nosing around

explanation.surface: A cheese lover wonders whether to bother competing when they can't even get a sniff of the Stilton.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue cheese is marked with blue streaks like veins, and the adjective means veined or full of veins.

clue.text: Hang about Ohio to dip into volume from Thurber?

indicators.note: one letter dips into the other word, going inside it

parts.note: James Thurber was American, so the volume measure gets its American spelling
O is the initial letter of Ohio, used as its abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone lingers in Ohio to dip into a book by the humorist James Thurber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Volume' looks like a book by Thurber, but it is a measure of liquid, spelt the American way because Thurber was American.
explanation.definitionFit: To hang about is to linger idly, a common synonym.

clue.text: In this, very much like others down the line, flabbergasted at censorship row

definitions.text: In this, very much like others down the line

indicators.note: flabbergasted means utterly thrown, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is astonished at a dispute over censorship.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cryptic description: in this practice the living revere their forebears, who are 'others down the line' of descent, very much as if they were gods.
explanation.definitionFit: This religious practice venerates forebears along the family line, so devotees think very highly of those who came before.

clue.text: A cart brought round for hangings

indicators.note: the cart is brought round the other word, enclosing it

parts.note: a dray is a low cart for heavy loads, such as a brewer's cart
per means for, as in so much per head

explanation.surface: A cart is wheeled round to carry hangings.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening 'A' is only part of the surface; 'cart' alone gives the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Hangings are curtains and other cloth hung in loose folds, which is what the word names.

clue.text: Maybe Eve maybe Adam has several weeks exciting — time's up!

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means at the top, so this letter comes first

parts.note: Adam is one example of a man, referred to as he

indicators.note: exciting means stirring up, so these letters are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: Eve and Adam spend several thrilling weeks together before their time runs out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'time's up' looks like the end of the fun, but it says T goes at the top of this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical phrase refers to women, so Eve, the first woman in Genesis, is an example.

clue.text: Arms not utilised in violent smash-and-grab!

definitions.text: Arms not utilised in violent smash-and-grab!

indicators.note: the letters of arms are not used, so they are taken out of the pool
violent means wildly disordered, so the remaining letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A smash-and-grab raid is carried out without weapons but with plenty of violence.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove A, R, M and S from SMASHANDGRAB and rearrange the rest. In British slang a squabble with no real blows is 'handbags', and handbags are what a smash-and-grab thief snatches.
explanation.definitionFit: Purses are typical loot in a street snatch, and British slang also uses the word for a scuffle where nobody truly fights.

clue.text: Respectable Oriental literary heroine master's lifted aboard spirited horse

parts.note: Oriental means eastern, abbreviated E

indicators.note: aboard means on board, so one piece rides inside the horse

parts.note: a steed is a lively riding horse

indicators.note: lifted means taken away, so the named letters are removed

parts.note: Emma is Jane Austen's heroine in the novel of that name
MA is a Master of Arts degree

explanation.surface: An eastern literary heroine is lifted onto a lively horse, making a respectable figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lifted' takes the master's degree out of Jane Austen's heroine, and 'aboard' seats what is left inside the horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Something held in high regard is considered respectable and worthy of honour.

clue.text: One lamenting boomeranged dog knocked out on resort

indicators.note: the dog's letters are knocked out of the longer word before rearranging
to re-sort is to sort again, so the remaining letters take a new order

explanation.surface: Someone grieves because a thrown boomerang knocked out their dog at a holiday resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort' looks like a holiday spot but reads as re-sort, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who bewails or complains about something is a lamenter.

clue.text: Ambassador touring strokes husky

indicators.note: touring means going round, so the ambassador's letters go round the other piece

parts.note: HE stands for His Excellency, the title of an ambassador
oars are rowers, called strokes in a crew

explanation.surface: An ambassador on tour stroking a husky dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'husky' suggests the sled dog, but it means rough-voiced.
explanation.definitionFit: A husky voice is rough and gravelly, as when the throat is sore.

clue.text: What may cut more slack, not taking sides

indicators.note: the sides are left and right, L and R, which are not taken

parts.note: laxer means looser or slacker

explanation.surface: Someone who stays neutral may allow more slack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sides' are left and right, L and R, the usual crossword pair.
explanation.definitionFit: A tool with a blade on a handle chops wood, so it is something that may cut.

clue.text: Hold back work behind bar

definitions.meaning: to suppress feelings, keeping them in
a barman restocks the shelves with bottles

explanation.surface: Someone holds off working behind a bar.
explanation.definitionFit: Suppressing emotion is keeping it corked, and a barman restocking bottles on shelves does exactly that job.

clue.text: In extra time, good header!

indicators.note: one letter goes in the other pieces

parts.note: a wide is a cricket extra, a run for a ball bowled too wide

explanation.surface: A footballer scores with a good header in extra time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'header' looks like football, but the device in a beer can produces the foamy head.
explanation.definitionFit: The gadget inside a canned beer releases gas to create a frothy head, so it is jokingly a header.

clue.text: Riot ignited by one warning ex-English captain to marshal force

indicators.note: to marshal is to gather troops together, so the captain's name gathers the other pieces inside

parts.note: John Terry is a former England football captain

indicators.note: ignited means set ablaze, so the letters are stirred up

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
an alarm is a warning

explanation.surface: A riot sparked by someone warning a former England captain to marshal his forces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ignited' shuffles RIOT and I to ITORI. This British reserve army is made up of volunteer part-time soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: This British volunteer reserve is a military force of part-time soldiers.

clue.text: Very wet valley needs to dry up

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means read from the bottom, so the word is turned around

parts.note: to air laundry is to dry it

explanation.surface: A soggy valley needs to dry out.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a drowned river valley, flooded by the sea, so it is very wet.
explanation.definitionFit: This coastal inlet is a river valley flooded by the sea, so it is literally drowned.

clue.text: Not quite What the Butler Saw? Lines extensively removed

indicators.note: not quite means the last letter is missing

parts.note: Joe Orton's play of that name is a farce
RY is short for railway, a set of lines

explanation.surface: A query whether a scene is not quite the Orton farce, with lines removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What the Butler Saw' is a farce by the English playwright Joe Orton; lose its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something very different or a long way from something else, so it is extensively removed.

clue.text: Bad spell of colic flu resulting in outgrowths

indicators.note: a bad spell means a poor arrangement of letters, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bad bout of colic and flu leads to unwanted growths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spell' looks like a period of illness, but here it is spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: These are small tufts or woolly outgrowths, such as bright patches on the sun's surface or tufts on plants.

clue.text: Strange to comprehend old Hindu dress that Lynn Anderson never promised you!

definitions.text: that Lynn Anderson never promised you!

indicators.note: to comprehend is to include, so the strange word contains the others

parts.note: rum is British slang for strange or odd
a sari is the draped garment worn by Hindu women

explanation.surface: A strange Hindu dress that a country singer never promised you.
explanation.walkthrough: Lynn Anderson's 1970 hit was 'I never promised you a rose garden'.
explanation.definitionFit: This formal garden is planted with roses, as in the song's promise that was never made.

clue.text: On LSD, perhaps? I get separate fixes on Ecstasy

indicators.note: get here means get placed into the drug's letters, so this letter is inserted too
the two pieces are fixed into the drug's letters at separate points, not side by side

parts.note: taken as written
EG, for example, means perhaps
E is slang for the drug Ecstasy

explanation.surface: A druggy question: on LSD, perhaps? I get separate fixes of Ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: EG goes after the L and I after the S. The on side is the cricket term for the half of the field behind the batsman's legs.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket the on side is another name for the half of the field nearer the batsman's legs.

clue.text: Not having the top end in bed?

indicators.note: in a down entry the top is the first letter, which is removed

parts.note: to end something is to kill it

explanation.surface: A puzzled query about whether someone in bed has reached the end without the top part.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is sick is often laid up in bed, so the question mark marks an example.

clue.text: 28 huntress failing to keep hold of American capital city

indicators.note: failing to hold means losing, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: the clue at 28 means swift, describing Atalanta, the fast huntress of Greek myth

explanation.surface: A swift huntress fails to keep hold of an American capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Atalanta was the swift-footed huntress in Greek myth who lost a race by stopping for golden apples.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the capital of the US state of Georgia.

clue.text: Period in which volume's penned by insecure ethologist about old plant

indicators.note: the period holds the rest inside it

parts.note: a dot is a full stop, called a period in America

indicators.note: penned means shut in, so the letter is held inside the anagram
insecure means unstable, so the letters are rearranged
about also signals the shuffle, turning the letters about

parts.note: V is the usual abbreviation for volume

explanation.surface: A shaky ethologist writes a volume during a period about an old plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'insecure' and 'about' rearrange the animal behaviourist's title with an O; 'penned by' shuts V inside that, and 'in which' puts it all within the period, a full stop.
explanation.definitionFit: This spring-flowering bulb, an erythronium, is a woodland flower, so it is a plant.

clue.text: 'Nothing' ex-English captain has 'left to give' — English winger

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing
Rio Ferdinand captained England's football team

explanation.surface: A former England captain has nothing left to give, like a spent winger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'winger' looks like a football wide player, but it is a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: This songbird flies on wings, so it is a winger in a cryptic sense.

clue.text: The closure of the Flower Festival

indicators.note: the closure is the end of the word, its last letter

parts.note: the aster is a daisy-like flower

explanation.surface: The flower festival comes to a close.
explanation.definitionFit: This Christian feast celebrates the Resurrection, so it is a religious festival.

clue.text: One overambitious, highflying Italian tenor short of oxygen

indicators.note: short of means lacking, so a letter is removed

parts.note: Enrico Caruso was a famous Italian tenor
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A highflying Italian tenor is short of breath.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth he flew too close to the sun on wax wings, which melted.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek mythical figure flew too near the sun on waxed wings, a byword for overreaching ambition.

clue.text: Co-ordinate one's appeal after a first degree

indicators.note: after places these pieces following the earlier ones

parts.note: a BSc is a Bachelor of Science, a first degree
one's reads as I'S, one is
SA is sex appeal

explanation.surface: Someone coordinates their appeal after getting a first degree.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry this is the horizontal coordinate of a point, measured along the x-axis.

clue.text: It's said to one dispensing with unnecessary layer

indicators.note: unnecessary means not needed, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: 'say when' is what you tell someone pouring you a drink

explanation.surface: A remark to a person peeling away a superfluous layer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'layer' looks like a stratum but is one who lays eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird that lays eggs is a layer, and the farm bird is the classic example.

clue.text: Oil-producer not well informed by institute

parts.note: ill means not well
up means informed, as in up on the news

explanation.surface: An oil producer, ill-informed, is guided by an institute.
explanation.definitionFit: This Indian tree, related to the mahua, yields an oil from its seeds, so it produces oil.

clue.text: Wherein those guilty of debt or larceny will accept shelter

indicators.note: accept means take in, so the stealing word holds the other piece

parts.note: larceny is theft
lee is a sheltered side, out of the wind

explanation.surface: Debtors and thieves will find somewhere to shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: This was a notorious London prison, used largely for debtors until 1844.
explanation.definitionFit: This old London jail held many debtors, so it is the place wherein debt defaulters were locked up.
